title: Short title, commencement and application
bareActText: (1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. (2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita. (3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India. (4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India. (5) The provisions of this Sanhita shall also apply to any offence committed by— (a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India; (b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be; (c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer resource located in India. Explanation.—In this section the word "offence" includes every act committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under this Sanhita. Illustration: A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in any place without and beyond India. He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found. (6) Nothing in this Sanhita shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any special or local law.
plainMeaning: This section names the code, says when it starts, and sets out who and where it covers. It applies to everyone for offences committed inside India, and reaches beyond India for Indian citizens anywhere, for anyone on Indian-registered ships or aircraft, and for anyone anywhere who attacks a computer resource located in India. It leaves army/special/local laws untouched.
ingredients: Short title: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
Central Government notifies commencement; different dates allowed for different provisions
Territorial application: offences committed within India
Extraterritorial: Indian citizens anywhere; persons on Indian-registered ships/aircraft; anyone targeting a computer resource in India
Savings clause for armed-forces mutiny/desertion laws and special/local laws
punishment: Not applicable — this section defines the code's title, commencement, and reach; it does not create an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to the title/extent provisions of the IPC; adds explicit extraterritorial reach over offences targeting a computer resource located in India.

illustrations: A, a citizen of India, commits a murder in a place beyond India. He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India where he is found.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.1 — verbatim text confirmed against the official Gazette (as published by UP Prosecution / India Code) and cross-checked via Rest The Case (Sep 2026).

title: Definitions
bareActText: In this Sanhita, unless the context otherwise requires, the following key terms are defined (40 clauses in all): "act" and "omission" (each including a single instance or a series); "animal"; "child" (a person below eighteen years); "counterfeit"; "Court"; "death"; "dishonestly"; "document"; "fraudulently"; "gender" (the pronoun 'he' applies to male, female or transgender); "good faith"; "Government"; "harbour"; "injury"; "illegal" and "legally bound to do"; "Judge"; "life"; "local law"; "man"; "mental illness"; "month" and "year" (Gregorian calendar); "movable property"; "number" (singular includes plural and vice versa); "oath"; "offence"; "person" (includes a company or association, incorporated or not); "public"; "public servant"; "reason to believe"; "special law"; "valuable security"; "vessel"; "voluntarily"; "will"; "woman"; "wrongful gain" and "wrongful loss" (and "gaining/losing wrongfully"). Words not defined here but defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000 or the BNSS, 2023 carry the meanings assigned there.
plainMeaning: Section 2 is the code's dictionary — 40 clauses fixing the exact meaning of the key words used everywhere else, so that terms like 'dishonestly', 'document' or 'public servant' mean the same thing in every chapter. Because it is really a glossary, the platform surfaces these terms through its Dictionary feature — see the chapter's Dictionary tab.
ingredients: Defines 40 key terms used throughout the Sanhita
Definitions apply 'unless the context otherwise requires'
The defined meanings carry across all chapters
Undefined terms take meanings from the IT Act, 2000 or the BNSS, 2023
punishment: Not applicable — this is a definitions clause, not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to the general definitions of the IPC, consolidated and updated (e.g. adding 'gender' inclusively, 'child', and modern cross-references to the IT Act and BNSS).

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.2 — section title and role confirmed against the official Gazette table of contents (NCRB/India Code). Individual definitions summarised; exact wording per the official Act.

title: General explanations
bareActText: Section 3 sets out general explanations that apply throughout the Sanhita. Among them: (a) throughout the code, every definition, penal provision and illustration is to be understood subject to the exceptions in the 'General Exceptions' chapter, even though those exceptions are not repeated; (b) an illustration to a section helps explain it but does not limit its scope; (c) the rules on gender and number apply — the pronoun 'he' and its derivatives apply to any person of any gender, and (unless the context otherwise requires) the singular includes the plural and the plural the singular; (d) where several persons act together in furtherance of a common intention, each is liable as if the act were done by him alone; and (e) the rules on the criminal responsibility of children — nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age, and nothing is an offence done by a child above seven and under twelve years of age who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct on that occasion. (Summarised from the general explanations; see the official Act for the full wording.)
plainMeaning: Section 3 gives the reading rules for the whole code. It tells you that the general exceptions always apply even when not repeated; that illustrations explain but do not limit a section; how to read gender and number; that people acting on a common intention are each fully liable; and it sets the age of criminal responsibility — a child under seven can never commit an offence, and a child between seven and twelve is not liable if too immature to understand the act.
ingredients: General exceptions apply throughout, even where not repeated in a section
Illustrations explain a provision but do not limit its scope
Gender: 'he' and derivatives apply to any gender; number: singular includes plural and vice versa
Common intention: each person acting together is liable as for his own act
Child under 7: nothing done is an offence
Child 7-12 of immature understanding: not liable
punishment: Not applicable — these are general explanations, not an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Consolidates the general explanations and the infancy rules previously spread across the IPC.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.3 — section title confirmed against the official Gazette table of contents (NCRB/India Code); infancy rule cross-checked via PRS India text. Full set of explanations summarised; see the official Act for exact wording.
